name: Yongkom
catalog_citation: Christensen, Steve. 2002. Organised Phonology Data: Yongkom (Yonggom, Yongom) Language [YON]: Kiunga - Western Province. SIL-PNG (PDF metadata: SIL PNG Branch). 6 pp; 'Data checked by: Steve Christensen January 2002'; printed 21 September 2004. Corroboration…
catalog_locator: OPD printed p.4 = PDF p.4, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'; file the copy we hold (the Internet Archive capture http://web.archive.org/web/201…
catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) This is an intonation language with stress being realized as loudness & pitch. Stress pattern is left-footed & left-headed and therefore always on the first syllable of the word. kabak [ˈkɑ.bɑk] ‘axe’ unitap [ˈu.ni.ˌtɑp] ‘bent’ kiamunɛ [ˈki.ɑ.ˌmu.nɛ] ‘like-that’ biaŋka+n+ɛwɛn [ˈbi.ɑŋ.ˌgɑ.nɛ.ˌwɛn] ‘you removed’ (Christensen 2002 OPD p.4) ... Corroboration, Christensen 2010:1: “Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word, and the language uses intonation rather than being a tonal language.”
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Yonggom (yong1280) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's single title hit (Glottolog 155352, 'How snake lost its feet') is an SIL-PNG vernacular storybook that matched on 'feet'; it is not about stress (priority none). Beyond the list of works with stress in the title, the Glottolog 5.1 dump gives three descriptive works by Steve Christensen: the 2002 SIL Organised Phonology Data (SIL URL dead, sil.org/pnglanguages an automated-access block-403, no archived copy at the Internet Archive), the 2000/2013 reference grammar (SIL archive 55514, 'Not Available Online'), and the 2010 discourse paper in Pacific Linguistics 616, which is open (ANU repository) and already held by the project; it states first-hand, p. 1: 'Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word, and the language uses intonation rather than being a tonal language.' Zahrer's 2023 Muyu dissertation (held by the project) carries Christensen 2013:4-5 with examples showing initial primary stress plus trochaic secondary stresses, and notes Drabbe 1954 reports final accent for the Ninati/Metomka dialects and that Kawip Muyu has no lexical stress. Acquisition priority: high for Christensen 2013 grammar and 2002 OPD (both SIL Ukarumpa only).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: extracted text of PDF p.9 = printed p.1, Christensen 'Yongkom discourse: ergativity and topic', sect. 1.2 Phonology: 'Primary stress is on the first syllable of the word, and the language uses intonation rather than being a tonal language.' Verbatim, exactly as reported (line 203 of). The other stress hits in lines 2052, 4822ff., penultimate/tense-suffix stress) belong to other papers in the volume (Umbu-Ungu etc.), not to Yongkom. READING: fixed: initial syllable agreed. NEW PRIMARY SOURCE RECOVERED: the SIL OPD the reader could not open exists as an Internet Archive copy of the old SIL-PNG pubs path: http://web.archive.org/web/20150427111340/http://www-01.sil.org/pacific/png/pubs/92847454…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of every word; the language is not tonal (intonation only).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in Christensen 2010. Zahrer 2023:51-52 reports second-hand that Christensen 2013:5's example transcriptions mark secondary stresses on alternate syllables after the initial one (['u.ni.,tap], ['bi.aN.,ga.nE.,wEn]), i.e. trochaic feet from the left.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Note Zahrer 2023: Drabbe 1954 reports final-syllable accent for the Ninati/Metomka dialects (Indonesian Muyu), and Zahrer finds no lexical stress in Kawip (Muyu); stress-attracting verb suffixes in Muyu. These concern Muyu (nort2916 etc.), not the PNG Yongkom described by Christensen.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('first syllable of the word'); one-sentence statement in a discourse paper, Kabom/Kagaip dialect spoken in the Yongkom villages along the Ok Tedi; author's own fieldwork 1991-2004.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement describes the Kabom/Kagaip dialect of Yongkom spoken in the villages along the Ok Tedi, Western Province, PNG (Christensen 2010:1), which is Glottolog yong1280. The Indonesian-side Muyu varieties (Kawip, Ninati, Metomka) described by Zahrer 2023 and Drabbe 1954 are separate Glottolog languoids (e.g. North Muyu nort2916) and are reported to differ (no lexical stress in Kawip; final accent in Drabbe's Ninati/Metomka).

new_statements.reading: Fixed initial (word-initial) primary stress, no lexical tone, for the Kabom/Kagaip dialect of Yongkom spoken along the Ok Tedi (author's own 1991-2004 SIL fieldwork). Corroborated by the carried report of Christensen's 2013 reference grammar (Zahrer 2023:51-52): initial stress realised by loudness and pitch, with trochaic secondary stresses in longer words. A fixed: initial syllable coding for a new yong1280 record would rest on this open, first-hand sentence; the 2013 grammar or the 2002 OPD would be the stronger source if either becomes reachable.

sources.citation: Zahrer, Alexander. 2023. A Grammar of Muyu. Doctoral dissertation, Westfaelische Wilhelms-Universitaet Muenster.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sect. 2.4.1 '(Lack of) lexical stress', pp.51-52 (PDF p.77): reports second-hand that Christensen (2013:4-5, Yongkom Reference Grammar, SIL ms.) has lexical stress 'always to be on the first syllable', realised as 'both increase in loudness and pitch', with example transcriptions showing trochaic secondary stresses (disyllabic foot, trochaic meter); Drabbe 1954 (Ninati/Metomka) has accent on the last syllable; Zahrer's own Kawip (Indonesian Muyu) data show no lexical stress, only stress-attracting verb suffixes -d and -n realised as pitch accent.

sources.quote: Zahrer 2023:51-52: 'Christensen reports the lexical stress (realised as "both increase in loudness and pitch" (p. 4)) always to be on the first syllable. Although he does not explicitly mention secondary stress, his example words comprise symbols for primary and secondary stress: (70) Christensen's (2013:5) lexical stress in Yonggom: ["ka.bak] axe, ["u.ni.,tap] bent, ["ki.a.,mu.nE] like-that, ["bi.aN.,ga.nE.,wEn] you removed, ["ka.na.,wa.na.,wan.di.,wEn] they surrounded. ... Christensen analyses Yonggom words to have metrical stress with a disyllabic foot and trochaic meter.'
sources.locator: Christensen 2013 pp. 4-5 as reported by Zahrer 2023, sect. 2.4.1, pp. 51-52
sources.note: Pages 4-5 state (per Zahrer 2023:51-52) that stress is always on the first syllable, realised by loudness and pitch, with transcriptions showing trochaic secondary stress; the fullest first-hand treatment.
